clinical_classification_presentation: Classical Dengue fever (DF)
source_pdf_title: National Guideline for Clinical Management of Dengue

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: A proportion of patients infected with dengue virus develop classical dengue fever characterized by high fever, severe headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia, arthralgia and rashes.
Leucopenia and thrombocytopenia are usually observed.

Although DF is usually benign, it could be an incapacitating disease due to severe headache and musculo-skeletal pains (break-bone fever). Occasionally, unusual haemorrhage such as gastrointestinal bleeding, hypermenorrhea and massive epistaxis may occur.
Therefore, patients with probable dengue illness should be closely monitored as it can develop DHF with time.

relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: High fever, severe headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia, arthralgia, rash, leucopenia, thrombocytopenia, severe musculoskeletal pain (break-bone fever), gastrointestinal bleeding, hypermenorrhea, massive epistaxis.

conditions_decision_logic.result: Probable dengue should be closely monitored because DHF can develop over time.

recommended_action: Closely monitor patients with probable dengue illness because DHF may develop over time
exclusions_or_missing_information: The passage does not specify the number of clinical features required for diagnosis, laboratory cut-offs for leucopenia or thrombocytopenia, or a confirmatory diagnostic procedure.

additional_information.previous_note: DF is usually benign but may be incapacitating because of severe headache and musculoskeletal pain. Unusual haemorrhage may occasionally occur.
additional_information.descriptive_source_interpretation: The passage describes clinical features associated with classical DF. The number or combination of features required for diagnosis is not specified. Leucopenia and thrombocytopenia are described as usually observed. Unusual haemorrhage is described as occasional, not as a mandatory diagnostic feature.

Dengue: Asymptomatic Infection and Undifferentiated Fever
clinical_classification_presentation: Asymptomatic infection; symptomatic infection—undifferentiated fever (3.1.1, 3.1.2 and 3.1.2.1)
source_pdf_title: National Guideline for Clinical Management of Dengue
relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: Asymptomatic infection: absence of symptoms or minimal symptoms; age under 15 years is a population-level context. Undifferentiated fever: mild, nonspecific febrile illness, especially in first (primary) dengue infection; clinically indistinguishable from other viral infections.

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: Majority of dengue virus infections are asymptomatic. However, age appears to influence the prevalence of symptomatic disease. The majority of infections in children under age 15 years are asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic.

Some of the patients infected with dengue virus, especially for the first time (i.e. primary dengue infection), may develop a nonspecific febrile illness with mild symptoms which are indistinguishable from other viral infections.

conditions_decision_logic.result: Asymptomatic dengue infection: infection is present without symptoms; the absence of symptoms is not itself evidence establishing dengue infection.
An infected patient may present with a mild, nonspecific febrile illness clinically indistinguishable from other viral infections; this is especially described in primary infection.

exceptions_contraindications.interpretation: Mild nonspecific fever or absence of symptoms cannot establish dengue infection.
exceptions_contraindications.action: Do not diagnose dengue solely from the presentation; consider clinical assessment and investigation evidence as appropriate.

recommended_action: Recognise asymptomatic infection and undifferentiated fever as possible presentations of dengue. Do not confirm dengue on the basis of no symptoms, age under 15, or mild nonspecific fever alone. For other symptomatic manifestations, retrieve the linked Classical DF and DHF cards.
exclusions_or_missing_information: The passage provides no diagnostic confirmation test, required symptom combination, severity cut-off, treatment, or monitoring schedule. The statement about children under 15 years is a population-level description, not a diagnostic rule. Expanded dengue syndrome is named in the section classification but is not described by these two excerpts.

asymptomatic_infection.frequency: Majority of dengue virus infections are asymptomatic.
asymptomatic_infection.age_association: The majority of infections in children under 15 years are asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic.
asymptomatic_infection.interpretation: Descriptive epidemiological observation, not an individual rule-out or confirmation criterion.

undifferentiated_fever.differential_limitation: Clinically indistinguishable from other viral infections.

symptomatic_infection_presentations.coverage: Listed in the classification overview; detailed presentation not part of these excerpts.

additional_information.rule_implementation_note: Only execute presentation rules when dengue infection is already established through other evidence. Treat unknown symptoms or infection status as unknown, not false.

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: The clinical manifestation of dengue infection varies according to the virus strain and host factors such as age, immune status, etc. Many patients infected with dengue virus remain asymptomatic.

Symptoms develop after an incubation period of 4-7 days (range 3-14 days) and symptomatic patients may have one of the following conditions:
• Undifferentiated fever
• DF
• DHF
• Expanded dengue syndrome (rare)

conditions_decision_logic.result: Symptoms typically develop after 4–7 days of incubation (reported range 3–14 days).
Asymptomatic dengue virus infection (Figure 12).
Symptomatic dengue infection: undifferentiated fever, dengue fever (DF), dengue haemorrhagic fever (DHF), or expanded dengue syndrome (rare).

source_pdf_title: National Guideline for Clinical Management of Dengue

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: Sudden onset, high grade, continued.
The body temperature is usually between 39 °C and 40 °C (102° F to 104° F).
The fever may be biphasic, lasting 2–7 days in the majority of cases.

relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: Sudden-onset fever, high-grade fever, continued fever, biphasic fever, temperature 39–40 °C (102–104 °F), fever duration 2–7 days.
exclusions_or_missing_information: The passage does not state that temperatures outside 39–40 °C or fever lasting outside 2–7 days exclude DF. Fever characteristics alone are not specified as a confirmatory diagnostic rule.

additional_information.descriptive_source_interpretation: Descriptive fever characteristics: temperature usually 39–40 °C (102–104 °F); fever may be biphasic and lasts 2–7 days in the majority of cases. These are not specified as mandatory diagnostic thresholds.

clinical_classification_presentation: Classical Dengue fever (DF) - rash characteristics and progression
source_pdf_title: National Guideline for Clinical Management of Dengue

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: first 2 to 3 days - Diffuse flushing or blanching erythema may be seen on the face, neck and chest
Third and fourth day - a conspicuous rash that may be maculo-papular or rubelliform.

Afebrile period or defervescence - Some patients have a confluent erythematous or petechial rash with small areas of normal skin, described as “isles of white in the sea of red” may appear over the dorsum of the feet, on the legs and on the hands and arms. Skin itching may be observed.

(A) Undifferentiated macular or maculopapular rash may occur over the face, thorax, abdomen, and extremities during the acute phase of dengue. The rash is typically macular or maculopapular and may be associated with pruritus.

(B) Convalescent rash is characterized by confluent erythematous eruption with sparing areas of normal skin. It is often pruritic. The rash typically occurs within one to two days of defervescence and lasts one to five days.

relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: Diffuse flushing, blanching erythema, maculopapular rash, rubelliform rash, confluent erythematous rash, petechial rash, spared areas of normal skin, itching, pruritus.
exclusions_or_missing_information: The rash stage cannot be matched reliably if the day of illness or timing of defervescence is unknown.

additional_information.previous_note: The source describes possible rash patterns and timing; it does not state that every patient with DF must develop a rash.
additional_information.descriptive_source_interpretation: Descriptive rash progression: first 2–3 days, diffuse flushing or blanching erythema may be seen; third or fourth day, a maculopapular or rubelliform rash may appear; during defervescence, some patients may develop a confluent erythematous or petechial rash with spared areas of normal skin. Convalescent rash typically occurs within 1–2 days of defervescence and lasts 1–5 days. These descriptions are not mandatory diagnostic conditions.

clinical_classification_presentation: Dengue warning signs (CDC 2024)
source_pdf_title: National Guideline for Clinical Management of Dengue

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage:
Warning signs of dengue fever: (CDC 2024)
• Intense continuous abdominal pain or pain when palpating abdomen
• Persistent vomiting (≥3 episodes in 1 hr or ≥4 in 6 hrs)
• Fluid accumulation (pleural effusion, ascites, or pericardial effusion)
• Mucosal bleeding (gums, nose, vagina [metrorrhagia or hypermenorrhea],
kidney [macroscopic hematuria])
• Altered mental status (irritability, drowsiness, Glasgow Coma Scale score <15)
• Hepatomegaly (≥2cm below costal margin)
• Progressive increase of the haematocrit (in at least 2 consecutive measurements
taken 6 hours apart

relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: Continuous abdominal pain, abdominal tenderness, persistent vomiting, fluid accumulation, mucosal bleeding, altered mental status, hepatomegaly, progressive haematocrit increase.

conditions_decision_logic.result: Intense continuous abdominal pain or pain on abdominal palpation.
Persistent vomiting meeting the guideline episode count.
Fluid accumulation.
Mucosal bleeding (examples listed in source evidence).
Altered mental status.
Hepatomegaly at least 2 cm below the costal margin.
Progressive haematocrit increase in at least two consecutive measurements six hours apart.

exclusions_or_missing_information: This passage lists dengue warning signs but does not specify the corresponding management, referral, or hospitalisation actions. These must be obtained from the relevant management section of the guideline.

additional_information.source_note: Warning signs from the guideline page 28, attributed there to CDC 2024. These rules flag warning signs, not a confirmed dengue diagnosis.
additional_information.descriptive_source_interpretation: Persistent vomiting: ≥3 episodes in 1 hour or ≥4 episodes in 6 hours. Fluid accumulation: pleural effusion, ascites, or pericardial effusion. Mucosal bleeding: gums, nose, vagina (metrorrhagia or hypermenorrhea), or kidney (macroscopic hematuria). Altered mental status: irritability, drowsiness, or Glasgow Coma Scale score <15. Hepatomegaly: ≥2 cm below the costal margin. Progressive haematocrit increase: at least 2 consecutive measurements taken 6 hours apart.
additional_information.field_mapping_note: Boolean findings must derive from documented patient observations. Unknown values must not be treated as false.

clinical_classification_presentation: Dengue Haemorrhagic Fever (DHF)
source_pdf_title: National Guideline for Clinical Management of Dengue

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: DHF occurs in a small proportion of patients with dengue infection.

Most DHF patients present with acute onset of high fever and associated symptoms similar to DF in the early febrile phase. Plasma leakage and abnormal hemostasis are the hallmarks of DHF which usually occurs around the defervescence (settling of fever). There is a possibility of developing shock (dengue shock syndrome) if the leakage is severe or due to significant bleeding in addition to leakage.
Therefore, patients with probable dengue illness should be closely monitored as it can develop DHF with time.
For efficient management of DHF it is important to understand its natural history and its dynamic nature.

Clinical course of DHF is stereotypic and consists of three phases:
• Febrile phase
• Critical phase (leakage phase)
• Convalescent phase
Note: Equilibrium phase is seen in some cases after critical phase

relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: Dengue infection; acute-onset high fever and DF-like symptoms during the early febrile phase; plasma leakage, abnormal haemostasis, significant bleeding, and possible shock around defervescence.

then.result: There is a possibility of developing shock (dengue shock syndrome) if leakage is severe or significant bleeding occurs in addition to leakage.

recommended_action: Recognise the dynamic clinical course of DHF and its three main phases: febrile, critical (leakage), and convalescent. Understanding the natural history of DHF is important for efficient clinical management. Closely monitor probable dengue illness for possible progression to DHF (see DEN-DF-DX-001, DF-MON-001).
exclusions_or_missing_information: This excerpt does not provide complete formal DHF diagnostic criteria, specific monitoring intervals, or detailed treatment and referral instructions for dengue shock syndrome. The three phases describe the clinical course and should not independently be used to confirm DHF. Detailed phase-specific clinical features and management require the corresponding guideline sections. A finding of severe plasma leakage, or significant bleeding in addition to leakage, indicates a possibility of dengue shock syndrome; it does not by itself establish a DSS diagnosis.

additional_information.descriptive_source_interpretation: Early febrile phase: symptoms may resemble classical DF. DHF hallmarks: plasma leakage and abnormal haemostasis, usually around defervescence. Severe plasma leakage or significant bleeding in addition to leakage may lead to dengue shock syndrome. The passage does not specify a complete diagnostic threshold or a mandatory combination of symptoms.
additional_information.natural_history: DHF occurs in a small proportion of patients with dengue infection. Its clinical course is dynamic, and understanding its natural history is important for efficient management.
additional_information.clinical_phase_note: The guideline describes three main phases of DHF. It additionally notes that an equilibrium phase is seen in some cases after the critical phase.

equilibrium_phase.classification: Additional phase noted by the guideline; not included among the three main phases.

clinical_classification_presentation: Differential diagnosis of dengue; clinical differentiation of dengue, chikungunya and Zika (Table 2)
source_pdf_title: National Guideline for Clinical Management of Dengue

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: Fever that has similar clinical feature of dengue like fever, rash, body ache, headache are its differential diagnosis. Clinical presentation of following infections has similarity with dengue fever:
Arboviruses: Chikungunya virus, Zika virus
Other Viral Infection: Measles, rubella and other viral exanthems, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), Enteroviruses, Influenza, Hepatitis A, Hanta virus.
Bacterial diseases: Meningococcemia, Leptospira, Enteric fever, Melioidosis, Rickettsial disease, Scarlet fever, Sepsis.
Parasitic Disease: Malaria.
Dengue, chikungunya, and Zika are all mosquito-borne viral diseases that can cause similar symptoms, such as fever, headaches, muscle and joint pain.

Table 2: Table showing clinical differentiation among dengue, chikungunya and zika. HIGH: Dengue—thrombocytopenia, progressive increase in hematocrit, leukopenia; Chikungunya—arthralgias; Zika—pruritus.

MODERATE: Dengue—anorexia or hyporexia, vomiting, abdominal pain, chills, hemorrhages (includes bleeding on the skin, mucous membranes, or both); Chikungunya—rash, conjunctivitis, arthritis, myalgias or bone pain; Zika—rash, conjunctivitis.

LOW: Dengue—retro-ocular pain, hepatomegaly, headache, diarrhea, dysgeusia, cough, elevated transaminases, positive tourniquet test; Chikungunya—hemorrhages (includes bleeding on the skin, mucous membranes, or both); Zika—adenopathies, pharyngitis or odynophagia.
Early laboratory confirmation of clinical diagnosis may be important because some patients progress within a short period from mild to severe disease and sometimes to death.

relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: Fever, rash, body ache, headache; muscle and joint pain.

conditions_decision_logic.result: Table 2 (page 37) lists thrombocytopenia, progressive increase in hematocrit and leukopenia under HIGH for dengue.
Table 2 (page 37) lists arthralgias under HIGH for chikungunya.
Table 2 (page 37) lists pruritus under HIGH for Zika.
Table 2 (page 37) lists anorexia or hyporexia, vomiting, abdominal pain, chills and hemorrhages under MODERATE for dengue.
Table 2 (page 37) lists rash, conjunctivitis, arthritis and myalgias or bone pain under MODERATE for chikungunya.
Table 2 (page 37) lists rash and conjunctivitis under MODERATE for Zika.
Table 2 (page 37) lists retro-ocular pain, hepatomegaly, headache, diarrhea, dysgeusia, cough, elevated transaminases and positive tourniquet test under LOW for dengue.
Table 2 (page 37) lists hemorrhages under LOW for chikungunya.
Table 2 (page 37) lists adenopathies and pharyngitis or odynophagia under LOW for Zika.

recommended_action: Consider the listed infections in the differential diagnosis of dengue (arboviruses, other viral infections, bacterial diseases, malaria) and use Table 2 to differentiate dengue, chikungunya and Zika. Early laboratory confirmation of clinical diagnosis may be important.

Dengue: Hemorrhages (includes bleeding on the skin, mucous membranes, or both)

Chikungunya: Hemorrhages (includes bleeding on the skin, mucous membranes, or both)

exclusions_or_missing_information: Table 2 is an image on the PDF page; its cells (HIGH/MODERATE/LOW per disease) are recorded item by item, so the three Table 2 passages are reconstructed from the table, not word-for-word text. For the chikungunya-versus-dengue comparison from the chikungunya guideline, see CHI-025 and CHI-026.

additional_information.source_page_mapping: Differential diagnosis and Table 2: page 37; early laboratory confirmation: page 38.

Dengue Laboratory Tests: Time and Frequency of Investigation
clinical_classification_presentation: Initial investigation choice by illness day and test-interpretation caveats
source_pdf_title: National Guideline for Clinical Management of Dengue
relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: Suspected dengue, illness day, first consultation, fever status, clinical severity and available laboratory results.

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: CBC and NS-1 Ag/ Anti-Dengue Ab should be done in all suspected dengue patients at their first visit depending on the day of presentation.
Within 5 days: CBC, Haematocrit, Dengue NS1 antigen, SGOT, SGPT
These tests should be done during first consultation to get the baseline characteristics like Haematocrit and complete blood count if the patient presented within 5 days of fever.
This antigen test may become negative from 4-5 days of illness.
Anti-dengue IgM can be detected after 5 days of the onset of fever and reaches highest level after 7 days of fever.
Basic investigations depend on day of illness. CBC and NS1 Ag up to day 5 and CBC and Dengue Antibody from day 6 onward will support the diagnosis.
Investigation: • CBC and Hct • NS-1 • SGPT/SGOT • CRP (level 4)

conditions_decision_logic.result: For presentation within first five days, obtain CBC, haematocrit, dengue NS1 antigen, SGOT and SGPT as listed on page 41.
From day 6 onward, CBC and dengue antibody testing support diagnosis.

exceptions_contraindications.interpretation: The NS1 antigen test may become negative from 4-5 days of illness.
exceptions_contraindications.action: Interpret the result according to illness day and other clinical findings.

recommended_action: For suspected dengue, select tests by illness day: days 1–5, CBC, Hct, NS1 antigen, SGOT and SGPT (page 41); day 6 onward, CBC and dengue antibody (page 45). Interpret test results with clinical context.
exclusions_or_missing_information: The guideline's stated test timing and monitoring recommendations should not be treated as proof that a patient has dengue. RT-PCR is listed as a method for laboratory confirmation; the source does not require it for every suspected patient.

additional_information.early_diagnostic_finding: Leucopenia is common in adults and children with dengue fever and has diagnostic implications in the early period (page 38).
additional_information.updated_from_pdf_page_45: Day-6-and-later testing is explicitly stated on page 45; earlier inference wording was corrected.
additional_information.crp_note: Page 46 includes CRP (level 4) in the outpatient investigation checklist; this card does not make it universally mandatory.

card_title: Dengue Laboratory Tests: WBC and Neutrophil–Lymphocyte Ratio
source_pdf_title: National Guideline for Clinical Management of Dengue
relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: CBC results containing WBC, neutrophil count and lymphocyte count, or a reported NLR.

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: Leucopenia is common in both adults and children with DF (Level 1) and has an important diagnostic implication in early period.
The change in total white cell count (≤5000 cells/mm3) and ratio of neutrophils to lymphocyte (neutrophils <lymphocytes) is useful to predict the critical period of plasma leakage (Level 6).
NLR (Neutrophil Lymphocyte ratio) <2 strongly correlates with low platelets indicating severity of disease and reversal of NLR >2 correlates with improvement of disease (Level 6).
This finding precedes thrombocytopenia or rising haematocrit.

conditions_decision_logic.result: Finding useful for predicting the critical period of plasma leakage
Correlates strongly with low platelet count and disease severity; not a standalone severity diagnosis
NLR reversal associated with improvement; does not guarantee recovery

recommended_action: Review the WBC count and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio on the CBC; leucopenia has diagnostic implications in the early period.

source_pdf_title: National Guideline for Clinical Management of Dengue
relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: CBC result containing platelet count.

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: Thrombocytopenia is observed in patients with DF & DHF.
The level of platelet count is correlated with severity of DHF (level 1).
Thrombocytopenia (<100,000/mm3) usually precedes/accompanies plasma leakage.

conditions_decision_logic.result: Thrombocytopenia; correlated with DHF severity and usually precedes or accompanies plasma leakage

recommended_action: Review the platelet count on the CBC; thrombocytopenia (<100,000/mm3) usually precedes or accompanies plasma leakage.

card_title: Dengue Laboratory Tests: Haematocrit (Hct) and Plasma Leakage
source_pdf_title: National Guideline for Clinical Management of Dengue
relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: Hct result and, if available, the patient’s actual baseline Hct. Age group and sex are needed only if considering the guideline’s assumed baseline.

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: Haemotacrit is most important tool in diagnosing and guiding effective treatment of dengue patient(Level 5).
Approximately 5-10% increase in Hct may occur due to high fever, anorexia and vomiting.
Rising haematocrit more than 10 % indicates starting plasma lekage and rising haematocrit by 20% from the baseline indicates established plasma leakage.
In critical phase / leaking phase haematocrit may not rise due to concomitant concealed or overt bleeding.
There is no data but it assumes that base line Hct in child, adult female and adult male are 35%, 38% and 40% respectively.

conditions_decision_logic.result: Indicates starting plasma leakage according to the guideline
Indicates established plasma leakage according to the guideline
Bleeding may prevent Hct from rising; a non-rising Hct does not exclude plasma leakage

exceptions_contraindications.interpretation: Hct may not rise during the critical or plasma-leakage phase when concealed or overt bleeding occurs concurrently.
exceptions_contraindications.action: Do not exclude plasma leakage solely because Hct is not rising. Interpret Hct alongside the clinical condition and serial measurements.

recommended_action: Use haematocrit change from baseline to assess plasma leakage (>10% rise: starting; 20% rise: established). A 5-10% rise may be due to high fever, anorexia and vomiting.
exclusions_or_missing_information: The guideline provides assumed baseline Hct values but states that supporting data are unavailable.

card_title: Dengue Laboratory Tests: NS1 Antigen Testing
source_pdf_title: National Guideline for Clinical Management of Dengue
relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: Suspected dengue; illness day; NS1 antigen result if already tested.

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: The Dengue NS1 antigen usually positive on first day of illness.
This antigen test may become negative from 4-5 days of illness.

Note: The sensitivity, specificity, positive, and negative predictive value of rapid dengue NS1 antigen test were 81.5%, 66.7%, 78.2%, and 71.1%, respectively whereas that of NS1 ELISA were 89.9%, 100%, 100%, and 94%, respectively.
Concordance of Rapid NS1 and NS1 ELISA with PCR was 75.5% and 94%.

conditions_decision_logic.result: This rule covers illness days 1-3. NS1 is usually positive on the first day, but the source does not guarantee positivity on every day in this range.
NS1 antigen test may become negative from 4-5 days of illness; interpret a negative result according to illness day and other clinical findings.

result.interpretation: Reported performance favours NS1 ELISA over rapid NS1 in these data. This comparison alone does not determine which test must be used for an individual patient.

exceptions_contraindications.interpretation: A negative NS1 result does not exclude dengue. NS1 is usually positive from the first day of illness but may become negative from days 4-5.
exceptions_contraindications.action: Consider the illness day and other clinical findings. The guideline lists CBC and dengue antibody testing from day 6 onward.

recommended_action: NS1 antigen is usually positive on the first day of illness and may become negative from days 4-5; consider test timing when interpreting the result.

additional_information.test_performance_note: Sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV and PCR concordance are the figures reported in the guideline. They should not be assumed to apply identically in every testing population.

card_title: Dengue Laboratory Tests: IgM and IgG Antibody Patterns
source_pdf_title: National Guideline for Clinical Management of Dengue
relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: Suspected dengue; illness day; IgM/IgG results and, if available, previous antibody results or relative antibody levels.

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: Anti-dengue IgM can be detected after 5 days of the onset of fever and reaches highest level after 7 days of fever.
It can be detected up to 1-3 months after dengue fever.

In primary dengue infection- anti-dengue IgM will be detected earlier than IgG which (IgG) will appear on the 9th or 10th day of illness. Level of this IgG may persist at low levels for life long, indicating past dengue infection.

In secondary dengue infection- higher levels of anti-dengue IgGand lower levels of anti-
dengue IgM are detected at 2nd week. The anti-dengue IgG levels detected lifelong.

conditions_decision_logic.result: Supports dengue diagnosis in the appropriate clinical context. IgM usually peaks after day 7 and may remain detectable for 1-3 months.

Pattern consistent with primary dengue infection: IgM becomes detectable after day 5 and before IgG, which generally appears around day 9–10. IgG may persist at low levels for life. This pattern alone does not definitively classify the infection.

Findings potentially consistent with secondary dengue: IgG detected before day 5 and both IgG and IgM positive after day 5, or higher IgG with lower IgM during the second week. These patterns alone do not confirm secondary dengue.

exceptions_contraindications.interpretation: Anti-dengue IgM may remain detectable for 1–3 months after dengue fever. A positive IgM result alone does not establish that the patient has a new acute infection.
exceptions_contraindications.action: Interpret IgM alongside illness duration, other test results and clinical findings.

exceptions_contraindications.interpretation: In primary dengue infection, IgG generally appears around day 9–10 and may persist at low levels for life. In secondary dengue infection, IgG levels may be higher and can also persist for life. A positive IgG result alone does not establish current acute dengue infection.
exceptions_contraindications.action: Interpret IgG alongside illness day, IgM results, previous test results and clinical findings.

recommended_action: Interpret anti-dengue IgM/IgG results according to illness day and the primary versus secondary infection pattern.

additional_information.primary_secondary_pattern_note: The accompanying figure and the written paragraph are both relevant. The text specifies higher IgG and lower IgM during the second week in secondary infection; the figure depicts the IgG pattern from early illness. Both should be retained as source evidence.

source_pdf_title: National Guideline for Clinical Management of Dengue
relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: Suspected dengue; illness day; RT-PCR result if testing has already been performed.

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: Dengue diagnosis is confirmed by detecting DEN viral RNA using reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR; This test is usually positive within 5 days of onset of symptoms. It can also be detected by traditional PCR.)
Confirmed Case: Laboratory confirmation through any one of the followings
Positive RT-PCR or NS1 antigen test

conditions_decision_logic.result: Positive RT-PCR meets the guideline's laboratory confirmation criterion for dengue. The test is usually positive within 5 days of symptom onset.

then.timing_note: Usually positive within 5 days of symptom onset.

recommended_action: RT-PCR can be used to confirm dengue by detecting viral RNA; it is usually positive within 5 days of onset of symptoms.

source_pdf_title: National Guideline for Clinical Management of Dengue
relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: Plasma leakage or severe dengue with shock has been identified through clinical assessment.

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: During plasma leakage period Hct should be monitored at least twice daily and more frequently considering the clinical scenario, If facilities available.
Bedside haematocrit is suggested in admitted patients.
A regular haematocrit is more important for management than the platelet count
Even in severe dengue especially with shock haematocrit to be monitored 3 hourly or more frequently is crucial for management.

then.frequency: At least twice daily; more frequently according to clinical circumstances and available facilities.
Every 3 hours or more frequently according to the clinical scenario.

recommended_action: Monitor haematocrit at least twice daily during plasma leakage (more often if the clinical scenario requires); in severe dengue with shock, every 3 hours or more frequently.

card_title: Dengue Laboratory Tests: Serial Platelet and Laboratory Follow-up
source_pdf_title: National Guideline for Clinical Management of Dengue
relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: Current platelet count and previous platelet count, if available; clinical context and other laboratory results.

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: Follow up testing may be done on 1st afebrile day, but should be done daily once DHF is suspected.
Once the platelet count begins to rise and reaches ≥ 50,000/mm3,daily lab evaluations may be discontinued.

if_condition_data_missing.result: Do not assume that the platelet count is rising. Keep the recommendation available for evaluation when the missing information is obtained.

recommended_action: Follow-up tests may be done on the first afebrile day and daily once DHF is suspected; daily laboratory evaluations may be discontinued once the platelet count begins to rise and reaches ≥50,000/mm3.

additional_information.implementation_note: A rising platelet trend requires a previous platelet count for comparison.

card_title: Dengue Biochemical Tests: AST and ALT
source_pdf_title: National Guideline for Clinical Management of Dengue
relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: Suspected dengue or dengue severity assessment; AST (SGOT), ALT (SGPT) and laboratory-specific upper limits of normal.

conditions_decision_logic.result: AST higher than ALT is a commonly described transaminase pattern in dengue; it is not a standalone diagnostic criterion.
The guideline describes AST/ALT elevations of approximately 2–5 times the upper limit of normal in classical dengue fever. This range alone does not establish the clinical classification.
The guideline describes ALT/AST elevations of approximately 5–15 times the upper limit of normal in dengue haemorrhagic fever. This range alone does not establish the clinical classification.

exceptions_contraindications.interpretation: AST/ALT elevation patterns described for classical dengue fever and DHF are source-reported associations, not standalone diagnostic criteria.
exceptions_contraindications.action: Interpret transaminase results alongside clinical assessment and other investigations.

recommended_action: Assess AST and ALT against the laboratory-specific reference ranges. Consider AST being higher than ALT and the reported degree of enzyme elevation as supporting findings, not independent confirmation of dengue or DHF.
exclusions_or_missing_information: The source excerpt does not provide a universal numerical upper limit of normal for AST or ALT. The laboratory-specific reference range is needed to calculate multiples of the upper limit of normal.

additional_information.transaminase_ranges_note: The source gives 2–5 times the upper limit of normal for classical dengue fever and 5–15 times for DHF. The ranges meet at 5 times the upper limit of normal; this source overlap has been preserved rather than resolved.

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: Transaminases are commonly abnormal in dengue fever where classically AST is more than ALT.
Elevated aspartate aminotransferase levels were strongly associated with severe dengue. (Level 1)
In Classical Dengue fever AST/ ALT may be slightly raised (2-5 times of upper limit of normal) but in dengue haemorrhagic fever ALT and AST may be 5 to 15 times the upper limit of normal.

card_title: Dengue Biochemical Tests: Serum Albumin and Plasma Leakage
source_pdf_title: National Guideline for Clinical Management of Dengue
relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: Suspected dengue or plasma leakage assessment; serum albumin result.

conditions_decision_logic.result: Indicates plasma leakage according to the guideline.

recommended_action: Check serum albumin; <3.5 g/dL indicates plasma leakage.
exclusions_or_missing_information: The source gives serum albumin <3.5 g/dL as indicating plasma leakage; it does not state further albumin-based criteria.

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: Serum Albumin <3.5 gm/dl indicates plasma leakage.

card_title: Dengue Tests: Coagulation Profile
source_pdf_title: National Guideline for Clinical Management of Dengue
relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: Suspected DHF, DSS or severe dengue.

conditions_decision_logic.result: Reduction in coagulation and fibrinolytic factors is described in DSS.
aPTT is prolonged in about half of DHF cases according to the guideline; this finding alone does not diagnose DHF or DSS.
PT is prolonged in about one third of DHF cases according to the guideline; this finding alone does not diagnose DHF or DSS.
TT is also prolonged in severe cases according to the guideline.

exceptions_contraindications.interpretation: Prolongation of aPTT, PT or TT is described as an associated finding in DHF or severe cases; it is not, by itself, a guideline confirmation test for dengue or DSS.
exceptions_contraindications.action: Interpret clotting abnormalities alongside clinical assessment and dengue-specific confirmation criteria.
exceptions_contraindications.note: Interpretive limitation, not a direct quoted contraindication.

recommended_action: Coagulation profile (aPTT, PT, TT) may show prolongation in DHF and severe cases; interpret in clinical context.
exclusions_or_missing_information: The source does not give numerical thresholds for prolonged aPTT, PT or TT.

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: Assays of coagulation and fibrinolytic factors show reduction in DSS cases.
Activated Partial thromboplastin time (aPPT) and prothrombin time (PT) are prolonged in about half and one third of DHF cases respectively.
Thrombin time (TT) is also prolonged in severe cases.

card_title: Dengue Biochemical Tests: Additional Tests by Severity
source_pdf_title: National Guideline for Clinical Management of Dengue
relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: Dengue with severe clinical scenario, prolonged shock, DHF or DSS.
recommended_action: Depending on the severity of the clinical scenario, additional tests may be needed: serum creatinine/BUN, serum electrolytes, VBG, RBS and serum calcium.
exclusions_or_missing_information: The source does not give numerical thresholds for elevated creatinine/BUN, hyponatraemia, metabolic acidosis, low RBS or hypocalcaemia.

additional_information.implementation_note: Where a numerical threshold is unavailable, do not invent one; use the laboratory-reported interpretation or reference range.

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: Additional following test might be needed depending on the severity of clinical scenario:
Serum Creatinine/Blood urea nitrogen (BUN) may be elevated in prolonged shock.
Serum Electrolyte: Hyponatremia is frequently observed in DHF/DSS
VBG (venous blood gas analysis): Metabolic acidosis is frequently found in cases with prolonged shock
RBS may be low in DSS
Serum calcium: Hypocalcaemia (corrected for hypoalbuminemia) has been observed in DHF.

card_title: Dengue Tests: Chest X-ray and Ultrasonography for Plasma Leakage
source_pdf_title: National Guideline for Clinical Management of Dengue
relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: Suspected plasma leakage or DHF; need for objective evidence of fluid accumulation.

conditions_decision_logic.result: Pleural effusion on chest X-ray indicates fluid accumulation; it is not by itself confirmation of dengue.
Ultrasonography can provide objective evidence of fluid accumulation associated with capillary plasma leakage.

exceptions_contraindications.interpretation: Pleural effusion or ascites may provide objective evidence of fluid accumulation or plasma leakage; the finding alone does not confirm dengue infection.
exceptions_contraindications.action: Correlate with clinical dengue suspicion and confirmation evidence.
exceptions_contraindications.note: Interpretive limitation, not a direct quoted contraindication.

recommended_action: Use chest X-ray and ultrasonography to obtain objective evidence of fluid accumulation / plasma leakage; point-of-care ultrasonography is not essential but is a reliable method in clinically suspected DHF.
exclusions_or_missing_information: The source does not give detailed imaging criteria.

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: Chest X-Ray: Pleural effusion on X-ray in dengue indicates fluid accumulation.
Ultrasonography: To detect pleural effusions or ascites, it is essential to obtain objective evidence of selective capillary plasma leaking into the chest and abdominal cavities.

Point of care ultrasonography is not essential to manage dengue patient but it has now evolved into an important and reliable method of diagnosing plasma leakage objectively in clinically suspected DHF patients. (Level 4)

card_title: Dengue Tests: Excluding Other Diagnoses
source_pdf_title: National Guideline for Clinical Management of Dengue
relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: Fever where another diagnosis (malaria, enteric fever) needs to be excluded.

tests: Blood culture to exclude enteric fever

recommended_action: Other tests may be done to exclude other diagnoses, such as ICT or microscopy for malaria and blood culture to exclude enteric fever.
exclusions_or_missing_information: The source does not state when each exclusion test is required. Malaria and enteric-fever exclusion testing is not independently diagnostic of dengue; the previously repeated unrelated generic exception has been removed.

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: Other tests might be done to exclude other diagnosis such as ICT for malaria, microscopy for malaria, Blood culture to exclude enteric fever.

card_title: Dengue Tests: Urine, Cardiac and CSF Tests for Complications
source_pdf_title: National Guideline for Clinical Management of Dengue
relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: Suspected dengue with myocarditis, encephalitis or urinary abnormality.

conditions_decision_logic.result: Albuminuria or haematuria may be present; these findings alone do not confirm dengue.

exceptions_contraindications.interpretation: The guideline states that albuminuria/haematuria may be present; these findings alone are not a confirmatory dengue test.
exceptions_contraindications.action: Assess with the overall clinical findings and appropriate dengue confirmation tests.
exceptions_contraindications.note: Interpretive limitation, not a direct quoted contraindication.

recommended_action: Urine R/M/E may show albuminuria/haematuria; ECG, echocardiography, troponin I and CK-MB if myocarditis is suspected; CSF in dengue encephalitis.
exclusions_or_missing_information: The source gives no diagnostic thresholds for these tests.

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: Urine R/M/E: Albuminuria/Hematuria may be present
ECG, Echocardiography, Troponin I, CK-MB
CSF: In dengue encephalitis.

card_title: Dengue Tests: Effect of Medications on Liver Function and Clotting
source_pdf_title: National Guideline for Clinical Management of Dengue
relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: Patient has taken analgesics, antipyretics, anti-emetics or antibiotics.

exceptions_contraindications.interpretation: The guideline notes that analgesics, antipyretics, anti-emetics and antibiotics can interfere with liver function and blood clotting.
exceptions_contraindications.action: Review medication exposure when interpreting liver function and coagulation-related findings.
exceptions_contraindications.note: Directly supported caution from the source; no drug-specific effect or adjustment invented.

recommended_action: When interpreting liver function and clotting tests, take into account that analgesics, antipyretics, anti-emetics and antibiotics can interfere with them.
exclusions_or_missing_information: The source does not name specific drugs or say how to adjust interpretation.

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: N.B: It should be noted that the use of medications such as analgesics, antipyretics, anti- emetics and antibiotics can interfere with liver function and blood clotting.

card_title: Dengue Case Definitions: Suspected, Probable and Confirmed
clinical_classification_presentation: Dengue Case Definitions: Suspected, Probable and Confirmed
source_pdf_title: National Guideline for Clinical Management of Dengue
relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: Acute febrile illness; clinical or serological evidence and confirmatory test results if available.

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: Suspected case: Acute febrile illness meeting clinical dengue criteria without confirmatory tests.
Probable Case: Acute febrile illness with serological diagnosis.

Confirmed Case: Laboratory confirmation through any one of the followings • Positive RT-PCR or NS1 antigen test • Positive immunohistochemistry from necropsy tissues • Seroconversion (negative to positive IgM/IgG in paired sera) • Fourfold rise in IgG in paired sera samples.

conditions_decision_logic.result: Suspected case: acute febrile illness meeting clinical dengue criteria without established confirmatory evidence; missing/unknown test status does not satisfy this condition.
Probable case: acute febrile illness with serological diagnosis.
At least one of the page-45 laboratory confirmation methods is present.

recommended_action: Distinguish suspected, probable and confirmed case definitions using the page-45 criteria.
exclusions_or_missing_information: Clinical dengue criteria for suspected case are referenced but not fully defined in this paragraph; absence of confirmatory testing is not itself a positive test. A missing/unknown confirmatory-test field must not be treated automatically as false. Classification rules can overlap while test data are updated; confirmed evidence must be evaluated explicitly. The status field is an application-level representation of evidence, not an additional PDF diagnostic criterion; do not derive not_established from missing data or absence of a recorded test.

confirmation_status_mapping.not_established: Explicitly established that no qualifying confirmatory evidence is available on assessment (including testing not performed or inconclusive/negative testing as clinically interpreted).
confirmation_status_mapping.confirmed: One or more page-45 confirmatory methods is positive.
confirmation_status_mapping.unknown: Confirmation status has not been sufficiently assessed; do not assume not_established.

additional_information.classification_precedence: Confirmed evidence takes precedence over provisional suspected/probable labels in the application; retain provenance for positive serology and confirmatory tests.

card_title: Dengue Severity Classification
clinical_classification_presentation: Dengue Severity Classification
source_pdf_title: National Guideline for Clinical Management of Dengue
relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: Patient with suspected dengue for assessment of warning signs, severe plasma leakage, bleeding and organ involvement.

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: Dengue without warning signs: Fever (2-7 days) with two or more of the followings; nausea, vomiting, rash, aches and pains, positive tourniquet tests, or leucopenia (WBC <5000/mm3)
Dengue with warning signs: Dengue fever with any one of the warning signs. (page 28)

Severe Dengue: • Severe plasma leakage leading to shock (DSS) or fluid accumulation causing respiratory distress. • Severe bleeding as per clinical evaluation • Severe organ involvement (e.g. elevated AST/AST≥ 1000iu/L, impaired consciousness, or organ failure.

conditions_decision_logic.result: Fever for 2–7 days with at least two distinct source-listed features, without warning signs and without established severe dengue criteria; an incomplete assessment must not be interpreted as negative.
Dengue fever with any page-28 warning sign and no established severe dengue criteria; check severe disease before selecting the final category.
Severe dengue criteria listed on page 45; elevated AST ≥1000 IU/L is given as an example of severe organ involvement.

recommended_action: Classify severity with page-45 definitions, using page-28 warning signs for the warning-sign pathway.
exclusions_or_missing_information: The passage does not give a full scoring method or define severe bleeding quantitatively. Do not infer severe disease from isolated nonsevere laboratory changes. The features count must represent distinct source-listed features, not repeated entries. Severe organ involvement AST criterion is an example, not the only possible manifestation. The severe_dengue_criteria_present field is a derived application state; nonsevere labels require sufficiently documented absence of severe criteria. This is a safety rule-engine gate, not an added guideline definition.

additional_information.warning_sign_field: Use warning_signs_present consistently; ascertain from page-28 warning signs (DEN-WS-REF-005). Unknown is not false.
additional_information.severity_precedence_note: If severe dengue criteria are met, do not let a simultaneous nonsevere classification override severe disease; mutually exclusive final classification requires an application-level precedence policy.

feature_count_definition.note: Count each distinct listed feature at most once; treat repeated mention of one feature as one. WBC strictly <5000/mm3 in page-45 severity definition; a missing feature assessment is unknown, not absent.

additional_information.severe_status_rule: Derive severe_dengue_criteria_present from verified clinical assessment and listed severe features. Do not set false merely because no severe feature was documented. The field gates only final classification, not an instruction to postpone clinical care.

card_title: Dengue Outpatient History and Physical Assessment
clinical_classification_presentation: Dengue Outpatient History and Physical Assessment
source_pdf_title: National Guideline for Clinical Management of Dengue
relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: Acute febrile illness assessed in a fever corner or outpatient department.

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: Fever corner should consist of a Triage Desk where fever patients will be registered and assessed based on duration of fever. • Then the patients can be seen by medical officers and managed accordingly.

Stepwise approach on outpatient management on dengue History: • Date of onset of fever/ illness • Date and time of last episode of fever • Oral intake • Warning signs • Diarrhoea • Bleeding including menstrual bleeding • Change in mental status /seizure /dizziness • Urine output (frequency, volume and time of last voiding) • Other important relevant histories: drug history, comorbidities.

Physical examination: • Mental status • Hydration status • Haemodynamic status • Tachypnoea/ acidotic breathing/ pleural effusion • Abdominal tenderness/ hepatomegaly/ ascites • Bleeding manifestation

All patients should be assessed in a stepwise manner to reach at the diagnosis, determine the severity and place of management. At the end of evaluation, attending physician should be able to assess the patient on following points.  Could this patient have dengue?  Are there any warning sign?  Is the patient having plasma leakage?  Is the patient in shock?  What is the haemodynamic and hydration status of the patient?  Are there any co-morbidities or high-risk conditions or adverse social condition?  Is hospitalization required immediately/early?

conditions_decision_logic.result: Assess illness timing, oral intake, warning signs, diarrhoea, bleeding, mental state, urine output, drug/comorbidity history and page-46 physical examination findings.
Assess possible dengue, warning signs, leakage, shock, hydration/haemodynamics, high risk and need for hospitalization.

recommended_action: Obtain structured history and physical examination before deciding outpatient or inpatient management.
exclusions_or_missing_information: No unique diagnostic confirmation threshold or definitive triage score is specified in the checklist.

card_title: Dengue High-Risk Conditions, Comorbidities and Social Risk
clinical_classification_presentation: Dengue High-Risk Conditions, Comorbidities and Social Risk
source_pdf_title: National Guideline for Clinical Management of Dengue
relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: Patient with suspected or diagnosed dengue being screened for increased risk or barriers to safe home care.

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: Patients at high risk for more severe disease and its complications may need admission even without the above criteria.  Pregnant women  Elderly  Obesity  Patients on anticoagulants

Patients with comorbid conditions:  Diabetes mellitus  Hypertension  Chronic renal failure  Established liver disease  Ischemic heart disease  Solid organ/bone marrow transplant  Active malignancies  Hemolytic diseases and other haemoglobinopathies  Peptic ulcer disease  Patients on steroid or NSAID treatment  Patients on anticoagulants
Patients with adverse social circumstances  Age <1 year or >65 years  Living alone or has poor access to healthcare facilities  Lack of transportation  Unstable housing  Extreme poverty

conditions_decision_logic.result: Any listed high-risk, comorbid or adverse social condition merits assessment of suitability for admission; this does not mean automatic admission.

recommended_action: Assess clinical risk, comorbidities and social circumstances when determining place of care.
exclusions_or_missing_information: The source does not define “elderly” or “obesity” in this high-risk list; age <1 or >65 is explicitly given only under adverse social circumstances.

adverse_social_conditions: Living alone or poor healthcare access
additional_information.age_boundary_note: The age bounds <1 year or >65 years are under adverse social circumstances in the source; do not apply them as universal definition of elderly.

derived_risk_field_for_triage.true_when: Any RISK-001 listed condition is established present; return a flagged status for clinician assessment, not automatic admission.
derived_risk_field_for_triage.false_when: All relevant risk groups have been assessed and excluded.
derived_risk_field_for_triage.unknown_when: Assessment is incomplete or a relevant input is unknown.

additional_information.avoid_double_counting: Anticoagulant use is listed twice in PDF page 46, under high risk and comorbidity; retain both source contexts but evaluate the patient flag once.

card_title: Dengue Table 7: Home versus Inpatient Management
clinical_classification_presentation: Dengue Table 7: Home versus Inpatient Management
source_pdf_title: National Guideline for Clinical Management of Dengue
relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: Assessment of warning signs, high-risk/comorbid/social status, vital signs, urine output and fresh CBC.

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: Table 7: Showing dengue patients who need inpatient/outpatient management.
Short duration of fever
Platelet ≥100x109/L
Hct: 35-40% or baseline
Home management as well as followed up and assessed regularly.
Present WS
Inpatient management
Settling of fever is not a sign of recovery. Some patients will start plasma leakage around defervescence.
Patients at high risk for more severe disease and its complications may need admission even without the above criteria.

conditions_decision_logic.result: Full low-risk profile illustrated by Table 7: consider home management with regular follow-up following clinical assessment; not an automatic disposition.

Flag any source-listed concerning factor for clinician inpatient assessment. Platelets below 100×10^9/L are a Table 7 inpatient-profile finding but must never alone mandate admission. At exactly 100×10^9/L both table rows overlap. This screening rule is not a disposition algorithm.
Page 46 says such patients may need hospital admission even without other admission criteria; clinician must assess.

recommended_action: Use the combined assessment including Table 7, warning signs, comorbid/social risks, vital signs, urine output and CBC to guide clinician placement.

home_profile.fever: Short duration or fever in past ≤48 hours

inpatient_profile.interpretation: This is a combined illustrative Table 7 row, not a requirement that all risk factors simultaneously be present.

exclusions_or_missing_information: Table 7 presents two illustrative profiles, not an exhaustive triage score or a complete algorithm for mixed findings. At exactly 100×10^9/L, the printed platelet inequalities (≥100 in home row and ≤100 in inpatient row) overlap. Do not decide admission from platelet count alone. Missing values are unknown, not negative. Absence of a complete Table 7 low-risk profile does not automatically prove a patient needs admission, and the row patterns must not overrule clinical deterioration or immediate-return criteria.

additional_information.screening_rule_note: TRIAGE-002 flags clinical risks for assessment, not direct automatic admission. Isolated platelet/WBC values are evidence requiring contextual interpretation, not a standalone admission trigger.
additional_information.platelet_boundary_note: Exactly 100×10^9/L occurs in both printed platelet ranges.

rule_semantics.TRIAGE-001: Illustrative home-profile match ONLY, not discharge clearance. All inputs must be explicitly known; no match does not imply inpatient care.
rule_semantics.TRIAGE-002: Trigger clinical assessment for possible inpatient care; any single input is a screening flag, not a mandatory hospitalization rule.
rule_semantics.TRIAGE-003: High-risk or social-risk states may justify admission even without other criteria, as stated on page 46.

additional_information.risk_field_source: high_risk_or_comorbidity_or_social_condition_present is a derived three-state field from DEN-RISK-001; unknown does not mean absent.

card_title: Dengue Home Care: Rest, Hydration, Urine Output and Diet
clinical_classification_presentation: Dengue Home Care: Rest, Hydration, Urine Output and Diet
source_pdf_title: National Guideline for Clinical Management of Dengue
relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: Dengue patient selected for home care after assessment of warning signs, coexisting conditions and social risks.

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: Patients without warning signs or coexisting conditions or social risk should get home based care through a register of dengue patient.
Adequate physical rest in comfortable clothing, and preferably under a mosquito net

Ensure adequate oral fluid intake of around 2400 ml for 24 hours (if the body weight is less than 50kg, give fluids as 2ml/kg/hour for 24 hours) and it is better to spread this amount of fluid across the day.
This should consist of fluid such as ORS, green coconut water, other fruit juices or soup which has electrolytes rather than plain water

Ensure adequate urine output. (Encourage to pass urine every 3-4 hours). It is useful to measure the urine output, if possible, and document with time, as any reduction in urine output can be easily identified.
If the appetite is good, patients encouraged to take light and nutritious food.
If the patient’s appetite is poor, forced feeding should not be done, as taking adequate amounts of liquid is sufficient during illness.
It is advisable to avoid red/ brown (i.e. dark) colored food (red dragon fruit, beet root)/ beverages to avoid confusion with blood-stained vomitus/ melaena)
Patient should be informed about warning sign. (page 28)

conditions_decision_logic.result: Give home-care advice covering rest/mosquito net, oral fluids, urine-output observation and appetite-appropriate nutrition.
Source states fluids at 2 mL/kg/hour for 24 hours when body weight is less than 50 kg; clinical suitability requires assessment.
Inform the patient/caregiver about dengue warning signs; consult page 28 for full list and page 48 for immediate-return indications.

recommended_action: For home-managed patients, support rest, electrolyte-containing fluids spread across the day, urine-output observation and light nutritious food as tolerated.
exclusions_or_missing_information: No adjustment algorithm for fluid restriction, renal/cardiac comorbidities, or dehydration severity is supplied; avoid automatic volume prescription without clinical assessment.

additional_information.oral_fluid_guidance: Around 2400 mL/24 hours; if <50 kg, 2 mL/kg/hour for 24 hours
additional_information.urine_prompt: Encourage passing urine every 3–4 hours and documenting urine output if possible

card_title: Dengue Home Medication Guidance and Precautions
clinical_classification_presentation: Dengue Home Medication Guidance and Precautions
source_pdf_title: National Guideline for Clinical Management of Dengue
relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: Dengue patient being managed at home, with current medication and anticoagulant/antiplatelet history reviewed.

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: Tepid sponging for fever
Do not exceed 3 gm/day of paracetamol. (60mg/kg/24hrs in child)
Warn the patient that the fever may not fully settle with paracetamol and advise not to take excess.
Anti-emetics and PPI/H2 receptor blockers if necessary.
Avoid all NSAIDS (including COX-2 inhibitors) and steroids.
Temporally withhold warfarin, aspirin, clopidogrel & dipyridamole, in patients who take these on long term basis. Take expert opinion where these drugs are necessary.

conditions_decision_logic.result: Tepid sponging and source-stated paracetamol maximum: adults 3 g/day; children 60 mg/kg/24 hours; caution against excess when fever persists.
Avoid all NSAIDs including COX-2 inhibitors and steroids according to this home-management section.
Guideline advises temporary withholding; obtain expert opinion when these drugs are necessary. Do not automate stopping a long-term medicine.

exceptions_contraindications.restriction: Avoid all NSAIDs (including COX-2 inhibitors) and steroids.
Expert opinion where antithrombotic medicines are necessary; do not infer universally safe discontinuation.

recommended_action: Use dengue-specific fever and medication precautions; clinician review is essential before withholding chronic antithrombotic therapy.
exclusions_or_missing_information: The excerpt does not provide an individual paracetamol dosing schedule, a protocol for restarting withheld medicines, or criteria for when antiemetics/PPI/H2 blockers are necessary.

medication_details.conditional_medicines: Antiemetics and PPI/H2 blockers if necessary
medication_details.long_term_antithrombotics: Source advises temporary withholding warfarin, aspirin, clopidogrel or dipyridamole; expert opinion if essential.

card_title: Dengue Home Follow-up and Daily CBC Monitoring
clinical_classification_presentation: Dengue Home Follow-up and Daily CBC Monitoring
source_pdf_title: National Guideline for Clinical Management of Dengue
relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: Dengue patient receiving home care with illness day and CBC findings available.

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: Review daily with CBC. First CBC should be done at least at the beginning of the third day of fever/illness (preferably with SGOT and SGPT).
These patients should be followed up until the patient become afebrile for 24-48 hours with stable clinical parameters. Usually, by seven days, most patients recover.
If any indication for hospitalization appears within this follow up period, patient should get admitted to hospital.

Note: Written instruction to the patient/carer giver will be provided in Bengali regarding management of the patient. Instructions will be given in Bengali about investigations timing and how and when they can communicate with physician either physically or phone call/WhatsApp. (Instructions of patient/caregiver is in annexure).

conditions_decision_logic.result: Review daily with CBC; first CBC at least by the beginning of the third day of fever/illness, preferably with SGOT and SGPT.

Once afebrile for at least 24 hours with stable clinical parameters, request clinician assessment against the source 24–48-hour follow-up window; do not automatically terminate monitoring, especially if deterioration or hospitalization indications are present.
If an indication for hospitalization arises during follow-up, guideline directs hospital admission.

recommended_action: Daily CBC review with first CBC by beginning of illness day 3; monitor until afebrile 24–48 hours with stable clinical parameters and admit if indicated.
exclusions_or_missing_information: The text does not give an objective definition of stable clinical parameters or a universal single-hour endpoint within the 24–48-hour interval. No fixed automatic stop time or clearance criteria beyond afebrile 24–48 hours with stable clinical parameters is established in the provided text.

additional_information.written_patient_instructions: Provide Bengali instructions on management, investigation timing and how/when to contact clinicians.
additional_information.endpoint_safety_note: HOME-MON-002 is a prompt for clinician review, not a rule for automatic discharge/closing follow-up. HOME-MON-003 (new hospital indication) must be evaluated regardless of fever status and takes priority for escalation.

card_title: Dengue Immediate Return and Hospitalization Warning Conditions
clinical_classification_presentation: Dengue Immediate Return and Hospitalization Warning Conditions
source_pdf_title: National Guideline for Clinical Management of Dengue
relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: Home-managed dengue patient developing deterioration, poor oral intake, bleeding, decreased urine or respiratory symptoms.

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: Advise patients to return to the hospital immediately, if they develop any of the following conditions: • Clinical deterioration with settling of fever • Inability to tolerate oral fluids • Severe abdominal pain • Lethargy or irritability / restlessness Bleeding tendency like abnormal vaginal bleeding, blood vomiting, black tarry stool, bleeding from nose and gum. Reduced urine output for the last 4-6 hours (<150-200 ml/ 4-6 hours if weight is 50kg or more) ● Cold and clammy extremities ● Difficulty in breathing.

card_title: Chikungunya: Fever Characteristics
clinical_classification_presentation: Fever description
source_pdf_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: Abrupt-onset fever, low to high grade, usually lasting 24–48 hours; temperature may reach 39–40°C, with chills and rigor.

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: The fever varies from low grade to high grade, lasting usually for 24 to 48 hours. Fever rises abruptly in some, reaching 39-40°C, with chills and rigor, no diurnal variation, usually subsides with use of antipyretics.

exclusions_or_missing_information: These are descriptive fever characteristics, not standalone confirmation criteria.

card_title: Chikungunya: Joint Manifestations
clinical_classification_presentation: Arthralgia and arthritis characteristics
source_pdf_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: Joint symptoms may begin with arthralgia or arthritis; commonly symmetric, affecting ankles, wrists and small hand joints. Migratory polyarthritis may occur; larger joints can also be affected. Pain may be worse in the morning and may recur after temporary relief. Joints with prior trauma or degeneration may be involved earlier and more significantly. The classical bending phenomenon was probably due to lower limb and back involvement, which forced the patient to stoop and bend forward.

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: The joint symptoms usually start with arthralgia or arthritis. Involvement is symmetric and often ankles wrists and small joints of the hand are the worst affected.
Migratory polyarthritis with effusions may be seen, but resolves in the majority. Larger joints like knee and shoulder and spine were also involved.
Pain tends to be worse in the morning, relieved by mild exercise and exacerbated by aggressive movements. The pain may be relieved for 2-3 days and then reappear in a saddle back pattern.

There is a tendency for early and more significant involvement of joints with some trauma or degeneration. The classical bending phenomenon was probably due to the lower limb and back involvement which forced the patient to stoop down and bend forward.

card_title: Chikungunya: Mucocutaneous Manifestations
clinical_classification_presentation: Rash and other skin or oral manifestations
source_pdf_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: Transient maculopapular rash commonly resolves within 48 hours. Other reported findings include vesiculobullous eruptions, angiomatous lesions, purpura, persistent photosensitive hyperpigmentation, stomatitis and oral ulcers. Epidermolysis bullosa is also seen in children.

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: Transient maculopapular rash is commonly seen, usually disappear within 48 hours. Other skin lesion may appear in the form of vesiculbullous eruption, angiomatous lesions and fewer had purpuras. Epidermolysis bullosa is also seen in children.
Most skin lesions recovered completely except in cases where the photosensitive hyperpigmentation persisted. Stomatitis and oral ulcers also observed.

card_title: Chikungunya: Neurological and Ocular Manifestations
clinical_classification_presentation: Neurological and ocular complications
source_pdf_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: Reported neurological manifestations include meningo-encephalitis, encephalitis, acute encephalopathy, Guillain-Barré syndrome and myelitis. Ocular manifestations include neuro-retinitis and uveitis. Ocular manifestations in the South India outbreak included granulomatous and nongranulomatous anterior uveitis, optic neuritis, retrobulbar neuritis and dendritic lesions; the majority of patients recover with good vision.

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: Neurologic manifestations of meningo-encephalitis, encephalitis, acute encephalopathy Guillain-Barré syndrome and myelitis were reported.
Neuro-retinitis and uveitis in one or both eyes may occur.

The main ocular manifestation associated with the recent epidemic outbreak of chikungunya virus infection in South India included granulomatous and nongranulomatous anterior uveitis, optic neuritis, retrobulbar neuritis, and dendritic lesions. Majority of the patients recover with good vision.

card_title: Chikungunya: Clinical Severity Classification
clinical_classification_presentation: Mild, moderate and severe clinical presentations
source_pdf_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: Mild: low-grade fever, mild arthralgia, mild focal myalgia, general weakness, skin rash or itching. Moderate: persistent low- to high-grade fever, moderate arthralgia or arthritis, generalised myalgia, hypotension, mild bleeding, retro-orbital pain or oliguria. Severe: persistent high-grade fever, severe arthralgia or arthritis, persistent vomiting or diarrhoea, altered sensorium, bleeding or shock due to persistent vomiting and diarrhoea.

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: Chikungunya fever is classified in to three categories based on severity of clinical presentation.
Mild: Low grade fever; Mild artharlgia; Mild focal myalgia; General weakness; Skin rash/itching.
Moderate: Low to high grade persistent fever; Moderate arthralgia /arthritis; Generalized myalgia; Hypotension; Mild bleeding; Retro-orbital pain; Oliguria.

Severe: Persistent high grade fever; Severe arthralgia/Arthritis; Persistent vomiting / Diarrhoea; Altered sensorium; Bleeding (GI bleeding due to use of drugs e.g. analgesics); Shock due to persistent vomiting and diarrhoea.

recommended_action: Use the source-listed clinical features to support severity assessment; do not infer an unlisted combination or threshold.
exclusions_or_missing_information: The guideline lists findings under each severity category but does not specify a formal rule defining how many findings are required for each category.

card_title: Chikungunya: Supportive Care and Management Advice
clinical_classification_presentation: Home supportive care, joint care, recovery advice and condition-specific complication advice (ophthalmic, neuropsychiatric, cutaneous)
source_pdf_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: Mild or moderate illness managed at home; joint pain; recovery from acute illness; ophthalmic, neuropsychiatric or cutaneous complications.

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: Mild and moderate cases can be managed at home. Severe cases should be managed at hospital.
Consume plenty of water with electrolytes (approximately 2 litres of home available fluids with salt in 24 hours).
Adequate rest in a warm environment
Cold compresses may help in reducing joint damage. Heat may increase/worsen joint pain and is therefore best to avoid during acute stage.
Refrain from exertion. Mild forms of exercise and physiotherapy are recommended in recovering persons.
In cases with ophthalmic symptoms complications, consult with ophthalmologists.
Cutaneous manifestations with topical or systemic drugs, and neuro-psychiatric problems with specialist care and drugs).

conditions_decision_logic.result: Cold compresses may help reduce joint damage. Avoid heat during the acute stage because it may increase or worsen joint pain.
In cases with ophthalmic complications, consult an ophthalmologist.
Neuropsychiatric problems require specialist care and drugs, as stated in the source.
The source describes topical or systemic drugs for cutaneous manifestations; the specific drugs are not named.

then.result: Consume plenty of water with electrolytes (approximately 2 litres of home-available fluids with salt in 24 hours), take adequate rest in a warm environment, and refrain from exertion.
Mild forms of exercise and physiotherapy are recommended in recovering persons.

recommended_action: For home care, advise fluids with electrolytes, adequate rest in a warm environment and avoiding exertion. For joint pain, cold compresses may help; avoid heat during the acute stage. Mild exercise and physiotherapy are recommended during recovery. If ophthalmic complications occur, consult an ophthalmologist; neuropsychiatric problems require specialist care; cutaneous manifestations are treated with topical or systemic drugs.
exclusions_or_missing_information: The source does not specify the duration of home management or detailed criteria for choosing among hospital rehydration fluids. It does not name the specific drugs for cutaneous manifestations.

card_title: Chikungunya: Hospital Medication and Treatment Guidance
clinical_classification_presentation: Hospital-specific treatment and medication guidance following clinical/admission assessment
source_pdf_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
relevant_symptoms_or_prerequisites: Hospital management following clinical/admission assessment; dehydration, secondary bacterial infection, or consideration of NSAIDs.

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: Assess for dehydration and institute proper rehydration therapy. (5% DNS, Normal Saline, & baby saline for paediatric cases)
Antibiotics can be used to treat secondary bacterial infection.

In general, the diagnosis of hypertension should be based on at least three blood pressure measurements per visit and at least two to three visits at 1–4-week intervals (depending on the BP level) to confirm the diagnosis of hypertension.

The diagnosis might be made on a single visit, if BP is ≥160/100 mmHg or there is accompanying evidence of hypertension mediated organ damage (HMOD) (e.g., hypertensive retinopathy with exudates and hemorrhages, or LVH, or vascular or renal damage).

When the initial SBP is between 140 and 159 mmHg, or the DBP is between 90 and 99 mmHg, repeat measurements should be performed on three separate occasions within a period of 1 to 4 weeks to determine whether a diagnosis of hypertension is valid. All measurements should be taken in the same arm.
If possible and available, the diagnosis of hypertension should be confirmed by out-of-office BP measurement (i.e., HBPM and/or ABPM).

In the initial evaluation, measurement of blood pressure should be performed in both arms. If the difference in readings between arms is more than 10 mmHg, repeat the measurements at 1–2 mins interval. If the difference in readings between arms remains more than 10 mmHg on the second measurement, measure subsequent blood pressures in the arm with the higher reading and it should be noted. If the difference is >20 mmHg, consider further investigation.

If hypertension is not diagnosed, measure the person's clinic blood pressure at least every 3 years subsequently, and consider measuring it more frequently if the person's clinic blood pressure is close to 140/90 mmHg.

exact_supporting_evidence_passages.passage: Some of the diseases which can be considered in differential diagnosis are:
Dengue fever: Severe backpain with purpuras or active bleeding might suggest dengue fever. Confirmatory laboratory diagnosis is possible.

Reactive Arthritis: In general, any arthritis that follows a febrile gastrointestinal or genitourinary infection (triggering microbes) is considered a reactive acute inflammatory arthritis if it lasts less than six months .The hallmark feature is enthesitis where collagenous structures such as tendons and ligaments insert into bone are involved. Oral mucosal ulcers are seen.
Serum sickness illness: Polyarthritis may be associated with a serum sickness type reaction caused by vaccine, medication or other viral infections
Rickettsial disease can present with fever, rash and joint pains. Confirm by serology.

Rheumatic fever: More common in the children and presents with fleeting (migratory) polyarthritis predominantly affecting the large joints. Modified Jones criteria should be the basis for diagnosis. Raised ASO titre and a history of recurrent sore throat are other points to be noted.
Malaria: patient can present with high fevers and may also complain of joint pains. Periodicity of fever and alteration of consciousness / seizures should prompt a diagnosis for malaria

Leptospirosis: Severe myalgia localized to calf muscles with conjunctival congestion/ or subconjunctival haemorrhage with or without oliguria or jaundice in a person with history of skin contact to contaminated water would suggest Leptospirosis

Periodicity of fever and alteration of consciousness / seizures should prompt a diagnosis for malaria.

Severe myalgia localized to calf muscles with conjunctival congestion or subconjunctival haemorrhage, with or without oliguria or jaundice, in a person with history of skin contact to contaminated water would suggest Leptospirosis.

recommended_action: Consider in the differential diagnosis: dengue fever, reactive arthritis, serum sickness illness, rickettsial disease, rheumatic fever, malaria and leptospirosis, using the features stated in the guideline. Confirmatory laboratory diagnosis is possible for dengue; rickettsial disease is confirmed by serology.
exclusions_or_missing_information: The source gives these as features that 'might suggest', 'should prompt' or 'would suggest' each disease; it does not give formal diagnostic criteria. Rheumatic fever diagnosis is based on Modified Jones criteria, which are not listed in the source. Rule conditions list the features as stated; no feature is required in every patient.
